lesson_1.title: Two Pointers: Reversing a List
task: Instead of using a single loop, the 'Two Pointers' pattern uses two separate trackers: one starting at the front, and one starting at the back. Let's use this to flip a list backwards without creating a new list!
Phase 1: The Setup
Open the 'Variables' tab. Create a variable `left` and set it to 0. Create a variable `right` and set it to the length of the list minus 1 (the last index).
Phase 2: The Meeting Point
Open the 'Loops' tab and grab a 'while' loop. We want this loop to keep running as long as `left < right`. When they cross, we are done!
Phase 3: The Swap & Move
Inside the loop, use the 'swap variable' block from the 'Variables' tab to swap the item at `arr[left]` with the item at `arr[right]`.
Finally, add 1 to `left` and subtract 1 from `right` so the pointers move closer to the middle. Return the `arr` at the bottom.
hints: Hint 1: Your 'left' pointer moves forward (+1), and your 'right' pointer moves backward (-1).
Hint 2: The 'while left < right' condition ensures you stop exactly at the middle. If you don't stop there, you will accidentally swap everything back to its original place!

lesson_1.title: Two Pointers: Segregate Evens and Odds
task: Let's push all the even numbers to the left side of a list, and all the odd numbers to the right side.
Phase 1: Setup
Just like before, set `left = 0` and `right = length - 1`. Start a `while left < right` loop.
Phase 2: Checking the Rules
Inside the loop, check if the left item is even (`arr[left] % 2 == 0`). If it is even, it's already in the correct place! Just add 1 to `left`.
Check if the right item is odd. If it is, it's also in the correct place! Just subtract 1 from `right`.
Phase 3: The Swap
If `left` is pointing at an odd number AND `right` is pointing at an even number, they are both in the wrong place! Swap them, then move both pointers inward.
hints: Hint 1: You will need a few 'If' blocks here. The first checks if the left side is good. The second checks if the right side is good.
Hint 2: Only swap if BOTH pointers are pointing to numbers that belong on the other side.

lesson_1.title: Two Pointers: Target Sum in a Sorted List
task: If a list is perfectly sorted, two pointers can find a target sum blazingly fast. No nested loops needed!
Instructions:
1. Define `two_sum_sorted(arr, target)`. Set `left = 0` and `right = length - 1`.
2. Start your `while left < right` loop. Add the two items together: `current_sum = arr[left] + arr[right]`.
3. If `current_sum == target`, return a list of their positions: `[left, right]`.
4. If `current_sum < target`, the sum is too small. Because the list is sorted, we can make the sum bigger by moving the left pointer up (`left += 1`).
5. If `current_sum > target`, the sum is too big. Make it smaller by moving the right pointer down (`right -= 1`).
hints: Hint 1: Think of it like a scale. If the weight is too light, slide the left weight to the right to make it heavier.
Hint 2: If the weight is too heavy, slide the right weight to the left to make it lighter.

lesson_1.title: Two Pointers: Moving Zeroes
task: Let's move all the zeroes in a list to the very end, while keeping the other numbers in their original order.
Instructions:
1. Define `move_zeroes(arr)`. This time, both pointers start at 0! Set `reader = 0` and `writer = 0`.
2. The `reader` pointer will scan the list using a `while reader < length` loop.
3. If `arr[reader]` is NOT zero, we want to save it! Swap `arr[reader]` with `arr[writer]`, and then add 1 to `writer`.
4. Always add 1 to `reader` at the end of the loop so it keeps scanning forward.
5. Return the array.
hints: Hint 1: The 'reader' pointer is like a scout running ahead to find numbers that aren't zero.
Hint 2: The 'writer' pointer stays behind, holding the spot where the next non-zero number should be placed.

lesson_1.title: Two Pointers: Valid Palindrome
task: A palindrome is a word that reads the same forwards and backwards. We can check this instantly by comparing the outside letters and moving inward.
Instructions:
1. Define `check_palindrome(word)`. Set `left = 0` and `right = len(word) - 1`.
2. Loop while `left < right`.
3. If the letter at `left` does NOT equal the letter at `right`, return `False` instantly.
4. If they do match, move `left` up by 1 and `right` down by 1 to check the next inner letters.
5. If the loop finishes and nothing mismatched, return `True`.
hints: Hint 1: You are checking the outer shell. If 'word[0]' and 'word[last]' match, you move inward to check 'word[1]' and 'word[last-1]'.
Hint 2: If the loop finishes completely, it means every single mirror pair matched perfectly!

lesson_2.title: Fixed Window: Highest-Grossing 3-Day Weekend
task: Imagine you have a list of daily store sales, and you want to find the highest-grossing 3-day window. You *could* recount every 3 days from scratch, but that's slow. Let's use a Fixed Sliding Window to just 'slide' the 3-day frame across the list!
Phase 1: The First Window
Define `max_weekend_sales(sales)`. First, use a loop to add up just the first 3 days (`sales[0] + sales[1] + sales[2]`). Save this as `current_sum`, and also set `max_sum = current_sum`.
Phase 2: Sliding the Window
Now, start a new loop at index 3 (the 4th day) and go to the end of the list. This represents our window sliding forward.
Phase 3: The Swap Trick
Instead of recounting 3 days, just add the new day coming into the window (`sales[i]`), and subtract the old day falling out of the window (`sales[i - 3]`).
If this new `current_sum` is greater than `max_sum`, update `max_sum`. Return `max_sum` at the end.
hints: Hint 1: Think of a picture frame over 3 numbers. When you slide the frame right, one new number enters the frame (add it!), and one old number leaves the frame (subtract it!).
Hint 2: By adding and subtracting just one number, we save the computer from having to recount the middle numbers every single time.

lesson_2.title: Fixed Window: Max Sunny Days in a Week
task: You have a long weather forecast. Let's find the 7-day period that has the most 'Sunny' days.
Instructions:
1. Define `max_sunny_week(weather)`. The window size (k) is exactly 7.
2. Loop through the first 7 days. If a day equals `'Sunny'`, add 1 to your `current_sunny` counter. Set `max_sunny = current_sunny`.
3. Loop from index 7 to the end of the list to slide the window.
4. If the new day coming in is `'Sunny'`, add 1. If the day falling out (`weather[i - 7]`) was `'Sunny'`, subtract 1.
5. Update `max_sunny` if `current_sunny` is higher. Return `max_sunny`.
hints: Hint 1: This is exactly like the sales task, but instead of adding numbers, we are adding 1 if the word is 'Sunny'.
Hint 2: Remember to check the day falling out of the window (index `i - 7`). If it was Sunny, you must reduce your count because it's no longer in your 7-day frame!

lesson_2.title: Fixed Window: Finding Smooth Averages
task: Let's smooth out a choppy graph of numbers by finding the maximum average over any 4-day window.
Instructions:
1. Define `max_average(arr)`. The window size is `k = 4`.
2. Find the sum of the first 4 numbers. Save it as `current_sum` and `max_sum`.
3. Slide the window from index 4 to the end. Add the new number, subtract the old number (`arr[i - 4]`), and update `max_sum`.
4. Return the highest average by dividing the `max_sum` by 4.
hints: Hint 1: You don't need to divide by 4 inside the loop! That wastes time. Just keep track of the highest sum, and divide by 4 at the very end.
Hint 2: Ensure you are returning a decimal (float), not just an integer.

lesson_2.title: Fixed Window: Count Good Windows
task: Instead of finding the maximum, let's count how many 3-day windows hit a total sales goal of 100.
Instructions:
1. Define `count_good_windows(sales)`. Window size is `k = 3`.
2. Sum the first 3 days. If the sum is `>= 100`, set `good_count = 1`, else `good_count = 0`.
3. Slide the window forward. Add the new item, subtract the old item (`sales[i - 3]`).
4. Every time the `current_sum >= 100`, add 1 to `good_count`.
5. Return `good_count`.
hints: Hint 1: This uses the exact same slide logic (add new, subtract old). You are just updating a counter instead of a maximum variable.
Hint 2: Check your sum condition inside the loop after every single slide.

lesson_2.title: Fixed Window: Custom Window Size
task: Let's make our sliding window flexible! Instead of hardcoding 3 or 7, we will let the user pass in `k` as the window size.
Instructions:
1. Define `dynamic_fixed_window(arr, k)`.
2. If `k` is greater than the length of the array, return `0`.
3. Loop from `0` to `k` to find the initial sum.
4. Loop from `k` to the end of the list. Add the new item, but this time subtract `arr[i - k]`.
5. Return the `max_sum` found.
hints: Hint 1: Wherever you typed a '3' or '4' in the previous tasks, use the variable 'k' instead.
Hint 2: The item falling out of the window is always at index `i - k`.

lesson_3.title: Dynamic Window: Shortest Streak to Hit Goal
task: A Dynamic Window (like a caterpillar) shrinks and grows based on rules. Let's find the shortest streak of days that reaches a specific sales target.
Phase 1: The Setup
Define `shortest_streak(sales, target)`. Set `left = 0`, `current_sum = 0`, and `min_len = 999999` (a very high number).
Phase 2: The Expansion (Head moves forward)
Use a 'for each index' loop to move a `right` pointer through the list. Add the sales of `right` to `current_sum`.
Phase 3: The Contraction (Tail catches up)
Inside that loop, add a `while current_sum >= target` loop! This triggers when we hit our goal.
While inside this inner loop: Update `min_len` if the current window size (`right - left + 1`) is smaller.
Then, subtract the `left` item from `current_sum`, and add 1 to `left` (the tail moves forward, shrinking the window). Return `min_len` (or 0 if it wasn't found).
hints: Hint 1: The 'right' pointer expands the window to grab more sales. The 'left' pointer shrinks the window to try and find a smaller streak that still meets the target.
Hint 2: Window size is always calculated as `right - left + 1`.

lesson_3.title: Dynamic Window: Longest Shopping Spree
task: You have a budget. Let's find the longest streak of consecutive items you can buy without going over your budget.
Instructions:
1. Define `longest_spree(prices, budget)`. Set `left = 0`, `current_spent = 0`, and `max_items = 0`.
2. Loop `right` through the prices. Add `prices[right]` to `current_spent`.
3. If you go over budget (`while current_spent > budget`), shrink the window! Subtract `prices[left]` from `current_spent` and add 1 to `left`.
4. After ensuring the budget is safe, update `max_items` if the window size (`right - left + 1`) is larger.
5. Return `max_items`.
hints: Hint 1: This is the exact opposite of the previous task! You expand until you BREAK the rule (go over budget), then you shrink the tail until the rule is fixed.
Hint 2: Only check/update the `max_items` variable AFTER the while loop has made sure you are back under budget.

lesson_3.title: Dynamic Window: Longest Sunny Streak
task: Let's find the longest consecutive streak of 'Sunny' days in a weather log. This is a very simple dynamic window that resets completely when it hits bad weather.
Instructions:
1. Define `longest_sunny(weather)`. Set `current_streak = 0` and `max_streak = 0`.
2. Loop through every day in the `weather` list.
3. If the day is `'Sunny'`, add 1 to `current_streak`. If `current_streak` is greater than `max_streak`, update `max_streak`.
4. If the day is NOT `'Sunny'`, the streak is broken! Reset `current_streak` to 0.
5. Return `max_streak`.
hints: Hint 1: This is a specialized, simplified dynamic window. The 'left' pointer is basically teleporting to the 'right' pointer every time the streak breaks.
Hint 2: Don't forget to reset the current streak to exactly 0 when it rains!

lesson_3.title: Dynamic Window: Streak with One Sick Day
task: Let's find the longest streak of 'Present' days, but we will forgive exactly ONE 'Absent' day in the streak.
Instructions:
1. Define `longest_attendance(arr)`. Set `left = 0`, `absences = 0`, and `max_streak = 0`.
2. Loop `right` through the array. If `arr[right]` is `'Absent'`, add 1 to `absences`.
3. While `absences > 1` (we broke the rule!), shrink the window. If `arr[left]` is `'Absent'`, subtract 1 from `absences`. Add 1 to `left`.
4. Update `max_streak` with the window size (`right - left + 1`).
5. Return `max_streak`.
hints: Hint 1: The window expands normally. If it swallows a second 'Absent', the rule is broken! The 'left' tail must pull forward until it spits out one of the 'Absent' days.
Hint 2: The window size `right - left + 1` includes the one forgiven sick day, which is exactly what we want.

lesson_3.title: Dynamic Window: The Alternating Streak
task: Let's find the longest streak of numbers that perfectly alternate between Even and Odd (e.g., [2, 3, 8, 7]).
Instructions:
1. Define `longest_alternating(arr)`. Set `left = 0` and `max_len = 1`. (If the array is empty, return 0).
2. Loop `right` from index 1 to the end of the array.
3. Check the pattern: If `arr[right] % 2` is exactly the same as `arr[right - 1] % 2`, the alternating rule is broken!
4. When the rule breaks, the window collapses. Snap the `left` pointer directly to the `right` pointer.
5. If the rule didn't break, update `max_len` with the window size (`right - left + 1`).
6. Return `max_len`.
hints: Hint 1: You only need to compare the current number to the number immediately behind it.
Hint 2: When two even numbers or two odd numbers sit next to each other, the streak dies, and a brand new streak begins at the current index.

lesson_4.title: Prefix Sum: Running Total
task: A Prefix Sum array keeps a 'running total' of everything seen so far. This makes answering math questions later incredibly fast.
Instructions:
1. Define `running_sum(arr)`. Create an empty list called `prefix` and a variable `current_total = 0`.
2. Loop through every number in `arr`.
3. Add the number to `current_total`.
4. Append the new `current_total` to your `prefix` list.
5. Return the `prefix` list.
Sample Outputs:
hints: Hint 1: If the input is [1, 2, 3], the output is [1, 1+2, 1+2+3].
Hint 2: Just keep adding the current item to a master total, and append that master total to a new list every single loop.

lesson_4.title: Prefix Sum: Range Query
task: If we want to know the total sales between Day 2 and Day 5, we don't need a loop! We can just take the running total at Day 5, and subtract the running total from Day 1.
Instructions:
1. Define `range_sum(prefix_arr, start, end)`.
2. We are given an array that is ALREADY a prefix sum (running total) array.
3. If `start == 0`, just return `prefix_arr[end]` (because there is nothing to subtract!).
4. If `start > 0`, return `prefix_arr[end] - prefix_arr[start - 1]`.
hints: Hint 1: If you want the sum of indices 2, 3, 4, and 5, you take the total sum up to 5, and subtract the total sum up to 1.
Hint 2: Because the array is already a running total, this requires zero loops! It is a fast O(1) math trick.

lesson_4.title: Prefix Sum: Finding the Balance Point
task: Let's find the 'Pivot Index' — the exact spot where the sum of the numbers on the left equals the sum of the numbers on the right.
Instructions:
1. Define `find_pivot(arr)`. First, find the total sum of the entire array using the list `sum` tool or a loop. Save it as `total_sum`. Set `left_sum = 0`.
2. Loop through `arr` using an index loop (`i`).
3. Calculate the right side: `right_sum = total_sum - left_sum - arr[i]`.
4. If `left_sum == right_sum`, return the index `i` immediately!
5. After the check, add `arr[i]` to `left_sum` before the next loop starts.
6. Return `-1` if no balance point is found.
hints: Hint 1: You don't need to constantly loop to find the right side. If you know the total weight is 100, and the left side is 20, and the middle item is 10... the right side MUST be 70!
Hint 2: Always update `left_sum` AFTER you do the equality check.

lesson_4.title: Prefix Sum: Highest Altitude
task: You are riding a bicycle. You are given a list of altitude *changes* (e.g., go up 5, go down 3). Find the highest altitude you ever reach. You start at altitude 0.
Instructions:
1. Define `largest_altitude(gain)`. Set `current_alt = 0` and `max_alt = 0`.
2. Loop through the `gain` list.
3. Add the altitude change to `current_alt`.
4. Update `max_alt` if `current_alt` is higher.
5. Return `max_alt`.
hints: Hint 1: This is just creating a running total and tracking the maximum value seen along the way.
Hint 2: Since you start at altitude 0, the maximum altitude could just be 0 if all you do is go downhill!

lesson_4.title: Prefix Sum: Splitting the Array
task: Given an array, how many ways can we split it into two parts so that the left part has a LARGER sum than the right part?
Instructions:
1. Define `ways_to_split(arr)`. Find the `total_sum` of the array. Set `left_sum = 0` and `valid_splits = 0`.
2. Loop through the array, but STOP before the very last item (we need at least one item on the right side!).
3. Add `arr[i]` to `left_sum`. Calculate `right_sum = total_sum - left_sum`.
4. If `left_sum > right_sum`, add 1 to `valid_splits`.
5. Return `valid_splits`.
hints: Hint 1: This is very similar to the Balance Point task. You keep a running `left_sum` and calculate the `right_sum` using subtraction.
Hint 2: Make sure your loop stops at `length - 1`. A split requires two valid sides.

lesson_4.title: Optimization Challenge: Maximum Water Area
task: You are given an array representing heights of vertical walls. We want to find the two walls that hold the most water between them.
Checking every possible pair of walls takes O(n²) time. Let's optimize this to O(n) using Two Pointers!
Optimization Guidelines:
1. Start `left` at 0 and `right` at the end of the array. Set `max_area = 0`.
2. Loop while `left < right`.
3. Calculate the area: The width is `right - left`. The height is the smaller of the two walls (`min(arr[left], arr[right])`). Area = width * height.
4. Update `max_area` if this area is larger.
5. The Optimization Trick: To find a potentially taller container, move the pointer that is pointing to the SHORTER wall inward. (If left is shorter, left += 1. Else right -= 1).
6. Return `max_area`.

lesson_4.title: Optimization Challenge: Dynamic Sliding Window Efficiency
task: When a sliding window breaks a rule, inexperienced programmers reset the left pointer all the way back to 0. A true sliding window NEVER moves backwards. It only slides forward.
Optimization Guidelines:
1. Open your 'Longest Shopping Spree' code.
2. Ensure your `left` pointer never resets to 0 inside the loop.
3. The `left` pointer should only ever move forward (`left += 1`) to shrink the window until the rule is fixed.
4. This guarantees that both pointers only travel the length of the array exactly once, proving an O(n) Time Complexity.
